open-question.question: `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` will name `codex exec "<prompt>"` as the Codex form of a headless line, whose Claude Code and Antigravity form is `-p "/cairn:<skill>"`. Codex's documented explicit invocation is the `$` sigil, which a shell expands as a variable inside double quotes, and whether Codex accepts `/cairn:<skill>` is unconfirmed. What prompt text, in what quoting, does the page give for invoking a cairn skill through `codex exec`?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It is Codex's documented explicit invocation with the namespace the README already shows, so users type one form everywhere, and single quotes stop the shell's `$` expansion with no escape character to lose, where a dropped backslash silently sends Codex a truncated prompt and an apostrophe in a goal fails loudly; a `codex debug prompt-input` render on the installed 0.159.3 passes `$` and `/` prompt text through alike and injects no skill for either, so no other form has evidence over the documented one.
open-question.alternative: The page gives `codex exec '$cairn:<skill>'` as the Codex form of a line. The prompt uses Codex's documented `$` sigil with the plugin namespace, which is the same `$cairn:<skill>` text the Codex README already uses. The prompt sits in single quotes so the shell passes the `$` through as written. The swap rule gains one more step: moving a line to Codex also rewrites `"/cairn:<skill>"` to `'$cairn:<skill>'`. The placeholder rule for `<goal>` changes from "no double quote" to "no single quote" on Codex lines. The command uses Codex's documented explicit invocation and the namespace the README already shows, so users type one form in both places. Single quotes are the plain POSIX way to stop `$` expansion and need no escape character that a reader could drop. It breaks the page's double-quote convention. A `<goal>` written in prose often contains an apostrophe, which ends the single-quoted prompt early, so Codex lines need a different placeholder rule from the other hosts. Whether `codex exec` resolves a `$cairn:` mention in its prompt text is still unconfirmed; it holds only if a no-model probe or the live verification checks it, and whether the live run is headless is a separate question.

alternative.id: Namespaced sigil, escaped in double quotes

open-question.alternative: The page gives `codex exec "\$cairn:<skill>"` as the Codex form of a line. The prompt uses the documented `$` sigil with the plugin namespace and stays in double quotes like every other line on the page, with the `$` backslash-escaped so the shell does not expand it. The legend says why the backslash is there. The swap rule adds rewriting `/cairn:` to `\$cairn:` inside the existing quotes. The "no double quote" rule for `<goal>` stays as it is. It keeps the page's one quoting convention and its placeholder rule for every host, so `<goal>` prose with apostrophes still works. It uses the same documented sigil and namespace as the README. The backslash is easy to lose when copying or rewriting a line. If it is lost, the shell silently expands `$cairn` to nothing and Codex receives `:<skill>`, with no error. The escape is POSIX-shell specific. It shares the open point that `$` mentions in `codex exec` prompt text are unconfirmed, which depends on the probes or the live verification.

The page gives `codex exec '$<skill>'`, the unnamespaced `$skillname` form exactly as Codex's skills page writes it, in single quotes so the shell leaves the `$` alone. The swap rule rewrites `"/cairn:<skill>"` to `'$<skill>'`, and Codex lines use the "no single quote" placeholder rule. It is literally the explicit-invocation form Codex documents, so it does not depend on whether Codex accepts a `plugin:` prefix inside a `$` mention. It differs from the namespaced `$cairn:` form the recorded README decision chose, so a user sees two forms. A bare name can collide with a same-named skill from another plugin or from `.agents/skills`. It shares the single-quote apostrophe problem and the unconfirmed resolution of `$` mentions in `codex exec`.

The page gives `codex exec "/cairn:<skill>"`, the same prompt text and double quoting as the Claude Code and Antigravity lines. The swap rule stays as recorded: change the binary invocation, drop `--model` and `--effort`, replace the permission flag, and leave the prompt as it is. There is no `$`, so nothing needs escaping. The prompt text is identical across all three hosts, so the recorded one-line swap rule works as written. It also matches the slash names that the rendered Codex skills use for each other unchanged. Nothing on this machine shows that Codex treats `/cairn:<skill>` as a skill invocation. `codex exec` probably passes it to the model as plain text, so the skill runs only if the model recognises the name. That is a model-judgment path, which the probe decision says the design should not lean on. It also contradicts the `$cairn:` form the README gives.

The page gives a plain-prose prompt that names the skill, such as `codex exec "Run the cairn:<skill> skill"`, in double quotes. It uses no sigil and no slash command and relies on Codex choosing the skill from its name and description. Arguments such as `<goal>` follow the prose. The swap rule rewrites the prompt into that sentence, and the "no double quote" rule stays. It needs no unconfirmed invocation syntax and no shell escaping. Codex documents that skills are picked implicitly from their descriptions, so the line does not depend on how `$` or `/` mentions are parsed in `codex exec`. Which skill runs, and whether one runs at all, is left to the model. Two runs of the same line can differ, which weakens a headless chain where nobody is watching. The prompt wording also becomes a new convention the page has to define and keep stable.

For now the page keeps `codex exec "<prompt>"` with the prompt text unspecified and states no Codex invocation form or quoting. It says only that the prompt invokes the skill. The concrete text and quoting are filled in later in this milestone, once a no-model probe (for example, `codex debug prompt-input` on a prompt with a mention) or the live verification has shown which form Codex resolves. Until then the swap rule covers only the binary and the flags. The page never publishes an invocation form that might not work. The choice rests on the probe evidence the milestone has already committed to gathering, not on guessing between unconfirmed forms. Until the evidence arrives, the page's Codex coverage has no runnable line and the swap rule is incomplete. The open choice comes back as unfinished documentation work. Whether it can close inside the milestone depends on a probe giving a clear answer or on the live run being headless, and the run mode is a separate question.
